glossary.meaning: A bishop, for us, is not an officer of some wider institution, dropped into a posting. He is given a people. He preaches to them and baptizes them, and when they fail it is not a problem he manages but a wound he carries. The charge runs both ways: he answers for his flock, and his flock can stand in front of his seat and refuse to leave until he hears them.

The lapsed are our own people who complied with the order to sacrifice during the persecution -- some by sacrificing, some only by paying for a certificate that said they had. They are not strangers and not enemies. They sat where we sit, and now they are asking to come back.
Discipline is the road; reconciliation is the arrival. What matters is that it is a road at all. There is an order to it, the order takes time, and everyone can see it.
For us, a confessor is one who was interrogated for the Name, did not deny it, and lived. In Cyprian's time, that standing could rival a bishop's own authority.
For us, communion is a formal standing within the one body. You can lose it, and be given it back. At the council of 256, Cyprian said no one would be put out of it for thinking differently.

A certificate is a letter from a confessor, given to a lapsed person. It asks for peace, or says peace is granted. Cyprian wanted each one to name the person. Some named one person 'with his friends.'

pull_quotes.text: I grieve, brothers, I grieve with you. My own integrity and my personal soundness do not lure me into soothing my griefs. That is because it is the shepherd who is wounded most deeply when his flock is wounded. I hold each one of you close to my heart, and I share the heavy burden of sorrow and mourning. I wail with those who wail, I weep with those who weep...

None of us sets himself up as a bishop over other bishops, and none of us uses a tyrant's terror to force a colleague into obedience. Every bishop has his own right to judge, in keeping with the freedom and power allowed to him. He can no more be judged by another bishop than he himself can judge another. Instead, let us all wait for the judgment of our Lord Jesus Christ. He is the only one who has the power both to place us in the government of His Church and to judge how we conduct ourselves there.

The visible form of a branch can exist even when it is separated from the vine. But the unseen life of the root can only be had in the vine. So the bodily sacraments can give “the form of godliness.” Even those who are separated from the unity of Christ’s Body carry and celebrate them. But the unseen, spiritual power of godliness cannot be in them at all. In the same way, feeling does not stay with a person's limb when it is cut off from the body.

You share communion with the members of the Apostles. You share communion with the shrines of the holy martyrs, who are spread over the whole world. And you belong to my care, so that I may give a good account of you. You know what my whole account is. “Lord, You know that I have spoken. You know that I have not kept silent. You know in what spirit I have spoken. You know that I have wept before You when I spoke and was not heard.”

cite.text: In our earliest years, those who had confessed Christ and suffered for it made a claim of their own. Their suffering, they held, gave them standing to ask peace for some who had failed the test they passed. We took that claim in earnest. Their suffering was real, and so was what it carried. And it still had to be answered by something steadier than one man's word, however real his suffering had been: a name set down, then examined before the whole congregation and with its judgment. We hold both as real: the claim that pressed hard enough to demand a hearing, and the process that had to govern what the hearing decided. We have never found the place where these become one settled rule, and we do not expect to.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: When someone wronged the community, how was it handled -- and could they come back?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: Their name is set down. Not a vague 'such a one with his friends', but one person, by name, whose change someone has actually seen. Then comes the waiting, and it is not a formality. What has genuinely changed in the person is watched and weighed, plainly, by someone answerable for weighing it rightly -- not granted the moment anyone feels moved to grant it, and not handed out on request. And at the end, it is not settled between the two of us alone. The same people who watched the failure are the ones who receive the person back, together, in the open. A door with no examination behind it is no door at all. It is just a room nobody ever really left.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: That sounds like you're making them prove themselves before you'll trust they've changed. Isn't real forgiveness supposed to be unconditional?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: We have asked ourselves that exact question, and we have never found the single answer that settles it without losing something true on one side or the other. A church that receives everyone back the same afternoon, no matter what, has no door at all -- the peace of the table stops meaning anything, because nothing was ever actually broken by breaking it. But a church that never receives anyone back has no Master either -- it has forgotten whose flock this was before it was ours to keep. So we hold both. The door is real, and it opens. And what walks through it is a person whose change has actually been seen, not merely claimed. We do not call that proving yourself to us. We call it being known well enough that your homecoming means something to the very people who watched you leave.

cite.text: We can argue that a colleague's ruling was wrong, at length, and still keep him at our table. One of our bishops said so when he opened the council that would settle the hardest question in the room. No bishop, he said, sets himself up as a bishop of bishops. None forces a colleague to obey. Every bishop has his own proper right of judgment. At that same council, he said we judge no one, and reject no one from communion, for thinking differently from us. A century and a half later, another of our bishops argued at book length that the ruling made that day was wrong. He never once put the man who made it outside our communion. In our own first years, we had seen separation from the inside. A deacon's faction gathered apart while our bishop was away in hiding. In those same years, a rival bishop was set up at Rome over a disputed election. We do not pretend those separations never happened. We hold our rule against separation knowing, from our own record, what it costs when it breaks.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: What did your people never settle?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: One question above all: what a font actually gives, when the hand that fills it comes from outside the one church. We have answered it twice, in two of our own voices, a century and a half apart -- and the two answers are opposites. One of us held that nothing valid is given outside at all. So the person comes to the water in the church, and is baptized for the first time. The other held that something real is given even there, though it does the person no good until they come inside -- so we bring them in, and let what they already carry begin to work. We do not resolve which of our own voices was right. Both asked the question in earnest, and neither could let it go unanswered.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: So which one do you actually believe?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: We hold both, and we are not going to pretend that is easier than it sounds. It matters too much to us for either answer to be true only in argument. What we can tell you is what is not in question either way: a font is never a small thing to us, however plainly someone asks about it. Everything else we hold rests on the answer to that question being real.

cite.text:
Between the two phases, the bishop's office changed its legal position. At first it had no legal standing at all. Later it could ask the state to act against a rival communion.

The outside change itself is documented. One element is contested: not whether the shift happened, but whether its consequence belongs among the world's inner forces or its outside pressures. Placing it as an inner force follows a judgement we made earlier, not a settled finding.

The shift is the old condition of illegality turned upside down, the same fact appearing at both ends of the story with the opposite sign. What a bishop could do had changed, though what a bishop was had not -- Cyprian never asked the magistrate for anything, and a century and a third later, the emperors could be asked, and eventually were.

We considered whether the shift itself was one of this world's own central concerns. It is not, because nothing in this world actually organizes itself around the shift. It changes the tools a bishop has, not what a bishop is. A separate look from the ethical and legal side reached the same conclusion. So it is kept as a real force, with an impact deliberately limited in proportion to its weight. A rival communion, the Donatist church, is what made the new state power worth using.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: The people who taught me the faith turned out to be hypocrites. Did that happen among you?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: Not exactly the shape of it. In our later years, one of our own voices moved across a hard question in three stages, and we report all three rather than the one that is easiest to defend. By his own later account, he first held that no one should be forced into the church. Argument only, never compulsion. Later, he and his colleagues in council asked the emperors for a narrow measure. It would fine rival clergy only where our own people had suffered violence. It was not even granted. Later still, he defended a fuller compulsion at length. He tells it as a change of mind. We report it as he tells it.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: So does that mean you think using force against them was right?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: We do not say it was self-evidently right, and we do not disown it either. What changed his mind, he says, was not the words of those who argued against him. It was the cases they could point to. The first was his own town. It had once stood wholly with the other side. Fear of the emperors' edicts brought it back to the one communion, and it stayed. Many other towns were named to him. That is what persuaded him, by his own account. We hold that position honestly, as his own, argued at real length. We are not ashamed to name it, and we do not ask you simply to accept it from us.

quiet.statement: The lapsed are the one group our whole first crisis was actually about, and they are the one group who left us nothing in their own words. We can tell you what was decided about a person who yielded under persecution, and how fiercely, and by whom. We cannot tell you why a person gave way, what they told themselves while they did it, or whether they judged the terms of their own return just. Every account we have of the lapsed is a bishop's account of them, written to decide what should be done, never their own.

who_speaks.text: Five figures carry this world's voice. Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, speaks in his own letters and books, as a shepherd wounded in his flock's wound. Pontius, his deacon, went with him into exile and wrote of his life and death. Celerinus, a confessor, wrote in the persecution, grieving for a sister who had sacrificed. Augustine, bishop of Hippo, preached to one congregation for decades. He argued with Cyprian across a century and a half. Possidius, his friend, stood by as he died.

documented_stories.teaser: Carthage makes a man its bishop while he is still new to the faith. Five of the clergy object. His deacon calls it God's judgment, shown in the people's favour.
documented_stories.tellable_as: How we came to treat a recent convert's own election, over his reluctance, as God's own judgment made visible
documented_stories.title: Chosen While Still New to the Faith

documented_stories.teaser: Celerinus grieves that his sister has sacrificed. He asks Lucian, a confessor held in prison, to grant peace. Lucian sends it back, on condition that each case goes before the bishop.
documented_stories.tellable_as: How one confessor asked another, not a bishop, to grant peace to women who had fallen
documented_stories.title: A Confessor Writes to a Confessor in Prison

documented_stories.teaser: Numidicus urges others to die for the faith and sees his wife burn with them. His daughter finds him alive under the stones. Cyprian adds him to the clergy of Carthage.
documented_stories.tellable_as: How our bishop added to our presbyters a confessor who had not wanted to survive
documented_stories.title: The Presbyter Who Had Not Wanted to Survive
documented_stories.when: Cyprian's years as bishop (the letter gives no year)

documented_stories.teaser: Christians are carried off as captives. The clergy and people of Carthage collect a hundred thousand sesterces to ransom them. No one knows whether the ransom worked.
documented_stories.tellable_as: How we sent a hundred thousand sesterces to ransom our captive brethren
documented_stories.title: A Hundred Thousand Sesterces for the Captives
documented_stories.when: Cyprian's years as bishop, 248/249 to 258 (the letter gives no year)

documented_stories.teaser: While the city flees its sick, Cyprian tells his people to help everyone, not only their own. Only his deacon's account keeps the sermon.
documented_stories.tellable_as: How our bishop met a plague by teaching us to love even our enemies, and to help everyone, not only our own
documented_stories.title: Love for Enemies in a Time of Plague

documented_stories.teaser: Two early texts tell how Cyprian was put to death, with his people watching. They agree on most of it, and differ on who tied the cloth over his eyes.
documented_stories.tellable_as: How two early texts tell the death of our great bishop Cyprian, and where they differ
documented_stories.title: Two Accounts of a Bishop's Death

documented_stories.teaser: The bishop who taught that even good Christians must repent before death has the psalms of penitence hung by his bed. He reads them and weeps.
documented_stories.tellable_as: How the man who taught that even good Christians must repent before death did it himself
documented_stories.title: Psalms of Penitence on the Wall
documented_stories.when: August 430, during the Vandal siege of Hippo

floor_note.text: This church confessed Jesus Christ, the only Son of God, our Lord. It went on to confess the Holy Spirit, completing the Trinity of the one Godhead. That faith did meet real opponents. Late in Augustine's years, an Arian bishop named Maximinus debated him at Hippo over the Trinity. But this church's sharpest arguments were rarely about the creed. They were about rites: who may baptize, whose baptism counts, and how someone who failed comes back to the table.

highlights.note: Christians who gave in to the order to sacrifice in 250. Some sacrificed, and some bought a paper saying they had.
Christians who were questioned, did not deny Christ, and lived. In Cyprian's time their standing could rival a bishop's.
Letters a confessor gave a lapsed person. They asked for peace, or said it was granted. Who decides was the quarrel.
Cyprian's phrase for what no bishop may be. Each bishop judges for himself and answers to Christ.
A real standing inside the one body. It can be lost and given back. Cyprian held it should survive sharp disagreement.
A rival church in the same North African towns, with its own bishops. It baptized again those who joined it.
The view Augustine fought, that a person's own effort is enough without grace. Whether Pelagius held it so is disputed.
The bishops met at Carthage under Cyprian in 256. They ruled that those baptized outside the church be baptized in it.
The Roman emperor who began a new attack on Christians in 257. Under his rule Cyprian was sent away, then put to death.
Cyprian's deacon. He went with him into exile and later wrote the story of his life and death.
Bishop of Calama and Augustine's friend for nearly forty years. He wrote the Life of Augustine.
A people who crossed from Spain into Africa in the late 420s. In 430 their army besieged Hippo.
The chief city of its province and Cyprian's see. Its ruins lie in today's Tunis, in Tunisia.
A port in North Africa, where Augustine was bishop. It is now the city of Annaba, in Algeria.
The town where Cyprian was held in exile under Valerian. Its site lies in today's Tunisia.

legacy.text: Augustine's books outlived this world. Inside his own church, nothing else depended on how the argument over grace came out. Later it became a foundation of Western Christian thought. Catholic and Protestant readers still draw on it, and they still disagree about what it means.

The church that kept both bishops' books kept Cyprian even where it judged him wrong, on baptism. This world has no single living heir. Its ordinary work, a pastor answerable for one local flock, stands behind much of the Western church from before that church divided.

read_first.note: Cyprian's book on those who gave way in the persecution of 250. It sets out the road back, and why the bishop holds it.
Cyprian's letters, with some written to him. They include two confessors' own letters and his account of his election.

source.author: Cyprian of Carthage
source.work: The Epistles (82 letters, including letters TO Cyprian from Rome, Cornelius, the confessors, and Firmilian of Caesarea)

read_first.note: The Life of Augustine, written by his friend Possidius, who was with him when he died.

relations_summary.text: The rival Donatist church shared this world's provinces and its century, and it appealed to Cyprian himself. The two answered one question in opposite ways. When bishops disagree past any agreement, do they keep communion or build a rival church? The Donatists built their own. This church kept its bond, even with the bishop it judged wrong. Its law looks different from an imperial church's, too. There, church law orders the relations of sees and the state. Here, it exists to bring a failed member home.

sourcing.text: This world has more of its own words than any other built here so far. Cyprian and Augustine both speak at length, as bishops of this church, not as quotations in an opponent's book. The problem is who else speaks. Almost no one outside the clergy left an account. No ordinary believer wrote about an ordinary Sunday. No woman's own writing survives, and none of the lapsed explained themselves. The churches are known mostly from one letter, not from digging. Most of the reading here is done in English translations from the 19th century.

story.text: This is the ordinary church of Latin-speaking Roman North Africa, from about 246 to 430, and it lived in two cities. Carthage was the chief see of its province and the largest Latin Christian city outside Rome. Hippo Regius was a port further along the coast, in the church province of Numidia. The name used here is a modern label, because this church had no special name for itself. It saw itself simply as the church, doing the ordinary work of caring for the people in front of it.

At its center stood one plain fact: a bishop was given a particular people, in one place, and he answered for them. He preached to them week after week, taught those preparing for baptism, washed them at the font and fed them at the table. When they failed, it was his own wound before it was a case to judge. Cyprian put it in one image: the shepherd is wounded most deeply when his flock is wounded. The tie ran both ways. The people could call a man to the office against his will, and they could crowd before his seat and refuse to go home.

Cyprian was a trained public speaker who turned to the church in about 246. Within two or three years the people of Carthage made him their bishop by acclaim. He was still newly baptized, and five presbyters, the clergy just below a bishop, opposed him. He later named what had put him there: the people's voice, joined to God's judgment. A century and a half later, Augustine's path ran the same way. In 391 the congregation at Hippo seized him and had him made a presbyter while he wept.

In 250 came the first persecution enforced across the whole empire by plan. It did not mainly demand that Christians give up their faith, but a recorded act of sacrifice to the gods, proved by a certificate. Some Christians sacrificed, and others paid to have the sacrifice recorded without making it. Both groups were called the lapsed. They were the church's own people, and now they asked to come back. To shut them out for good would say that one hour under pressure decides a life. To let them straight back would say the hour meant nothing.

So the church kept a road back. A failed member's name was set down, and what had truly changed in the person was watched and weighed. At the end, the same people who saw the fall received the person home, in the open. A rival claim pressed against this road. Confessors were Christians who had been questioned, had not denied Christ, and had lived. Some of them wrote certificates of peace for the lapsed, and Cyprian complained that thousands went out every day. He held that the church's peace was not any one sufferer's to give, and that tension was never fully settled.

Plague came too, from about 249 to 262. Cyprian's deacon Pontius describes a city where people fled the sick and left bodies where they fell. Cyprian called his congregation together and told them that caring for their own was nothing remarkable. They should help everyone, their enemies included. The plague produced no new rule and no new structure, only a sermon and a short book on dying called On Mortality.

In 256 Cyprian opened a council of African bishops on a hard question. If someone was baptized outside the church, was that baptism real? The council held that nothing valid is given outside, so such a person must be baptized in the church for the first time. Opening the council, Cyprian said that no bishop sets himself up as a bishop of bishops. Each has his own right to judge, and no one is put out of communion for thinking differently.

Persecution returned under the emperor Valerian. Cyprian was sent into exile at Curubis, and then brought back to trial. On 14 September 258 he was put to death by the sword. He had spent years deciding what to do with those who failed the first test. The second test took him, and he did not fail it.

Then this church's own voice goes quiet for about 133 years, from 258 to 391. Much happened in those years, but what survives of them comes mostly from the rival Donatist church and its opponents, not from this church's pastors. A few old sermons may date from that time, and they have not yet been studied. So the silence is held as an open question, not a settled fact.

The second voice is Augustine. He came to the faith in 386 and was baptized at Milan in 387. At Hippo he was made a presbyter in 391 and bishop in 395 or 396. He preached to the same congregation for decades, and many of his sermons survive. By then a rival church stood in the same towns, the Donatists, with their own bishops in the same sees. They baptized again those who came over to them, and they named Cyprian's ruling as their warrant.

Augustine answered the font question the other way. Something real is given even outside the church, he argued, though it does the person no good until they come inside. So such people were received, not baptized again. In his book On Baptism he argued at length that Cyprian's ruling was wrong. Yet he never placed Cyprian outside the church. Disagreeing with a colleague, even a revered one, was not a reason to separate. The font was answered twice, and both answers stayed inside one communion.

On using force against the rival church, Augustine's mind moved in three stages. By his own later account, he first held that no one should be forced into the church. Then he and his fellow bishops asked the emperors for a narrow measure, and it was not granted. Later still, he defended a fuller use of force that was already in place. He told it as a change of mind. Scholars still dispute whether it was one, or a later way of telling the story. Cyprian never asked the state for anything.

In the 410s and 420s a second fight took hold, over grace. Augustine argued that no one's own will, left to itself, is enough to stand right before God. Whatever good a person does was given to them first. He wrote thirteen works against what he called the Pelagian view. Whether Pelagius himself held that view in that form is disputed. This argument belongs only to Augustine's years, and Cyprian never argued it in those terms.

In 430 a Vandal army besieged Hippo, and Augustine fell ill in the third month of the siege. His friend Possidius, bishop of Calama, was in the house. He tells how Augustine had the shortest psalms of penitence copied out and hung on the wall, and read them from his bed, weeping. He died on 28 August 430, and this world ends with him.

voices.hedge: His own letters let us hear him directly, and at length. But the story of his rise and his death comes mostly from his deacon, who wrote in praise. That he was newly baptized when chosen rests on that one witness alone.
voices.text: Cyprian was a trained public speaker who turned to the church around 246. Carthage made him its bishop within a few years, while he was still newly baptized. He led his people through persecution, plague and schism. A large collection of his letters survives, with some written to him, along with treatises such as On the Lapsed. He spoke of a shepherd wounded in his own flock's wound. He was put to death under Valerian in 258.

voices.hedge: These letters survive only because Cyprian kept them, though they cut against his own case. Celerinus never names his sister. No word of hers survives.
voices.text: Celerinus was a confessor of Carthage. He had been put in prison and had not denied Christ. His letter to Lucian, another confessor in prison, survives with Lucian's reply. In it he grieves for his sister, who had sacrificed, and asks Lucian to help restore her. Neither man was yet a cleric. These two letters are the clearest lay voices this world kept.

voices.hedge: So much of Augustine survives that he can seem to be this world's whole voice. He is not. He was one bishop, writing about the people in front of him, and their own words mostly did not survive.
voices.text: Augustine came to the faith in 386 and was baptized at Milan in 387. In 391 the congregation at Hippo seized him and had him made a presbyter while he wept. He was bishop there from 395 or 396 until his death in 430. He preached, taught those preparing for baptism, and argued against the Donatists, the Manichaeans and the Pelagians. Until his last illness he did not stop preaching.

voices.text: Possidius was bishop of Calama and Augustine's friend for nearly forty years. He wrote the Life of Augustine. He was in the house at Hippo during the siege of 430, and he watched and prayed as Augustine died.

tile.text: From about 246 to 430, this was the ordinary church of two cities in Roman North Africa, Carthage and Hippo. Each congregation had one bishop, given a particular people and answerable for them. When a persecution in 250 made many of them give way, their bishop did not write them off. He set a road back, examined and walked in the open. Cyprian of Carthage held that road, and he was put to death in 258. A century and a half later, Augustine of Hippo argued that Cyprian had been wrong about baptism, but never called him an outsider. This church argued hard about the font, about councils and about grace, but always inside a bond it would not break. Both bishops speak at length in their own words. Almost everyone else is missing: the ordinary believer, the women, and the people who gave way.
